The World Cup enforcement posture is worth tracking precisely because it's publicly stated in advance. If ICE does make immigration arrests at or around venues, that will be measurable and it will directly contradict what Mullin said today.

The interview also covered the 76-day DHS shutdown that ended last month,the longest in the agency's history. Mullin says, the department had to stop being proactive: "We just have to choose missions." TSA lost 8.6% of its workforce. CISA lost 1,100 people over the past year.

DHS Secretary Markwayne Mullin told CBS News that ICE will not be at the FIFA World Cup to "round up" non-citizens but explicitly did not rule out arrests. ICE is expected to have a presence at all 11 U.S. host cities this summer.

What the data doesn't yet tell us: whether courts will consolidate these conflicting rulings into a durable standard, or whether individual outcomes will continue to depend on whether a specific recipient has a lawyer who can sue fast enough.

Federal judges have ruled in specific cases that deporting recipients with valid status is illegal. But the Board of Immigration Appeals ruled in April that DACA status alone is not sufficient to halt a deportation directly contradicting those rulings.

His case sits inside a larger pattern. Per DHS data cited by the Texas Tribune: at least 261 DACA recipients have been arrested since 2025, 75 of them in Texas. At least 86 have been deported. Of the current 500,000 DACA recipients nationally, more than 80,000 live in Texas.

José Contreras, a 30-year-old Texas DACA recipient from Edinburg, was deported to Honduras in January despite valid DACA status. ICE flew him back in April, then immediately detained him upon landing. He was released May 7. DHS says it still intends to deport him.

This is worth watching carefully heading into the Nov midterms. Immigration as a Republican asset depended on a specific grievance,chaotic border crossings, that has largely resolved. Whether interior enforcement generates the same political energy is an open empirical question.

The shift reflects a real policy change: illegal border crossings are down sharply. But the issue has moved from the border to the interior, deportations of people with no criminal record, deaths of U.S. citizens in enforcement operations, and a party divided on what comes next.

The legality is still being litigated. A federal judge in D.C. found in December that the operation was likely unlawful, but didn't block it. The gap between announced scale and operational reality is one of the clearest data points we have on distance between rhetoric and fact.

the DoD operation is projected at $73 million, per figures provided to Sen. Elizabeth Warren, up from a previously reported $40M estimate. Over the past year, 832 detainees have passed through on 100+ flights. This week, government staff outnumbered detainees roughly 100 to 1.
Trump promised 30,000 immigration detainees at Guantanamo Bay. As of May 11, the U.S. was holding 6. Capacity at the facility is 400 beds. Fewer than 2% were occupied.
